records.name: Russia
records.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Official assessments from a foreign body conclude that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation/gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 Aug 2026): affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia — including the autonomous republic of Chechnya — constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. External-protection framework, dated 2025-26.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Russia (Level 4 'Do Not Travel') includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols; the charges span administrative and criminal codes, and HRW calls on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Meduza (19 Jun 2025): after the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the non-existent 'international LGBT movement' as extremist, cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the past two years alone.

The Moscow Times (23 Jun 2025): arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 — a St Petersburg queer woman describes waking up to find herself 'a second-class citizen' after the Supreme Court's extremist designation.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russian man arrested for allegedly running LGBTQ+ travel agency found dead in custody' — detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business, found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russia's LGBTQ+ community is living in fear following new laws and court rulings, activists say' — the post-designation crackdown under Putin pushes people into silence, flight and self-censorship.
Foreign Policy (Aug 2024): 'Russia's New Queer Purge: The Court Decision Driving the LGBT Community Into Exile' — how the extremism designation fuelled a purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians.

records.name: Afghanistan
records.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban — the nation's current ruling movement — is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 Morality Law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026.

sources.summary: EUAA Country Guidance: Afghanistan, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons' (profile last updated Jan 2023, in guidance May 2024): treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious/social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty — the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU.

EUAA COI Report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 (Feb 2026): no legal protections for sexual orientation or gender identity before or after the 2021 takeover; the 'Morality Law' of 31 Jul 2024 specifically prohibits lesbianism, anal intercourse and enabling same-sex relationships; per Amnesty International, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report (Jan 26, 2022), 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans: Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

OutRight International report (Feb 14, 2023), 22 interviews Sep-Oct 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in-country: Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in early rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations — punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media.

DW feature (Oct 2, 2021): profiles a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave; documents street attacks on men coded as gay (clothing changed, confinement indoors).

JURIST feature (Nov 8, 2024) summarising the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan (formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen): reports systematic persecution after Aug 2021, noting that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework and that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) Law, dated 31 Jul 2024: the overseer must prevent listed 'evils' including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery, gambling and other offences.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

records.name: Mexico
records.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comp

sources.summary: HRW dispatch (31 March 2025) "Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges": calls on Mexico’s states to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many states now have LGR procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist state to state.

HRW report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024), Tabasco: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

The Guardian (18 July 2024): Mexico City’s Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

IACHR press release (2024): urges federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all LGBTI violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

LSE USAPP analysis by Caroline Beer (22 November 2024): Mexico’s progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors explicitly caution their earlier work must not be read as evidence LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

Global Affairs Canada travel advice for Mexico: "Exercise a high degree of caution" nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional "avoid non-essential travel" advisories (e.g. Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast); recently updated for Hurricane Polo.

records.name: Portugal
records.summary:
Portugal remains one of the world's safest destinations for transgender visitors. The 2018 self-determination law allows legal gender and name change without medical requirements (minors 16-17 with parental consent), bathroom access matching one's gender is legally protected, conversion therapy is banned (2024), intersex infant surgery is banned, and hate-crime law covers gender identity — within an EU rule-of-law environment with very low violent crime. Same-sex marriage since 2010.

Two caveats pull it just below its Iberian neighbour Spain. First, in March 2026 the Portuguese parliament approved in first reading three bills (backed by the governing PSD/CDS and the far-right Chega) that would repeal the 2018 self-ID law, reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion, and ban hormones for minors. As of the most recent reporting this is not yet final law — it is in committee, and a government technical opinion warned it may be unconstitutional — so the self-ID framework is still in force. sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026: Portugal drops one place to 12th at 67%; no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban, while a new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children. No score 67% below Malta/Iceland/Belgium but above most of Europe.
Público (March 2026, in Portuguese): the Portuguese Parliament (AR) approved PSD, Chega and CDS bills reversing the gender-identity law - first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Observador (Mar 2026): parliament debates rolling back the gender-identity regime; psychologists' order and trans groups call it 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta (trans woman killed by youths in Porto) against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Documents the political fight around the three roll-back bills.

Joint statement: IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warn three bills debated 19 March, voted 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans/intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; if adopted Portugal would lose at least 4 Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, Netherlands, Ireland and France - regression from a European reference point.

Forbidden Colours (20 Mar 2026): Parliament passed the roll-back proposals 124 to 79 (backed by Chega, governing PSD and CDS-PP), sending them to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; the proposals directly target Portugal's 2018 self-identification law. Called a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

KET Brussels (26 Mar 2026): in first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform that allowed self-declaration from age 16; human rights groups say it is dismantling the self-determination law.

TVI/IOL: committee-stage analysis (CIG) of the bills warns they worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; Bloco de Esquerda bill assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations. Legislative-process detail on the roll-back package.

The Portugal Brief (16 Aug 2026): Justice Ministry data show legal sex/name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon (per Expresso) - even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 self-determination law scrapped. Uptick before the expected tightening.
